content.title: Latin America and the Caribbean
content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation

content.text:
Latin America and the Caribbean stand at a pivotal crossroads. The region is endowed with some of the richest renewable energy resources in the world – abundant solar in Mexico and Chile, strong winds in Patagonia, expansive hydro resources in Brazil and the Andes, and emerging geothermal and green hydrogen opportunities. At the same time, it grapples with persistent inequality, energy poverty, climate vulnerability, and slow investment flows.

This lesson explores how the region’s vast energy potential can be harnessed to drive inclusive and sustainable development. Energy is not just a sector – it is an enabler. It powers schools and clinics, fuels jobs and industrial growth, supports digital inclusion, and provides resilience against disasters and shocks. Yet, 17 million people still lack access to electricity, and 78 million rely on traditional fuels for cooking – exposing deep energy access gaps that must be addressed if the region is to achieve the SDGs.

Despite having one of the cleanest electricity mixes globally (over 60% renewable), LAC remains heavily reliant on fossil fuels for transport and industry. The challenge now is twofold: ensuring universal access to modern energy and shifting energy systems toward resilience, equity, and sustainability.

By combining regional data, policy analysis, and forward-looking opportunities, learners will gain a holistic view of why sustainable energy is a cornerstone for economic transformation, climate action, and social justice across Latin America and the Caribbean.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: A: Development Context in Latin America and the Caribbean

content.text:
Latin America and the Caribbean is a region marked by both rich natural resources and persistent development challenges. While it boasts one of the cleanest electricity matrices globally – 41% hydropower, 8% wind, 6.2% solar – this green advantage coexists with structural inequalities, fiscal constraints, and energy poverty.

LAC remains one of the most unequal regions globally. Countries like Brazil, Chile, and Mexico have some of the highest inequality rates in the world.

Approximately 80% of the population live in urban areas, and the region faces unique vulnerability to natural disasters and climate shocks – 152 million people were affected by 1,205 natural disasters between 2000 and 2019. At the same time, the region holds exceptional potential in hydropower, solar, and wind, presenting a rare opportunity to leapfrog into a clean and just energy future.

The region's renewable energy potential, combined with smart finance, inclusive policies, and industrial innovation can transform these vulnerabilities into engines for inclusive growth and climate resilience.

content.intro: M1: Introduction to Sustainable Energy System Transformation
content.title: B: Energy Challenges in Latin America and the Caribbean

content.text:
The region has achieved a high electricity access rate of 97.6% as of 2021, but these gains are uneven.

17 million people, mostly in rural and Indigenous communities, remain unelectrified. In Haiti, for instance, only 47% of people have electricity access, and just 5% have access to clean cooking solutions.

Access is not just about lighting homes – it's about enabling education, health care, livelihoods, and climate adaptation. Last-mile electrification strategies, decentralized renewable systems, and digital tools (e.g., pay-as-you-go solar) present immediate and scalable solutions to enable a just energy transition 💬️

78 million people lack access to clean cooking, severely impacting health and disproportionately burdening women and girls.

Development Opportunity: Expanding energy access improves education, health, productivity, and gender equality. In rural areas, modern energy solutions reduce women's time poverty 💬️ and improve economic opportunities. Solar mini-grids, digital pay-as-you-go models, and off-grid solutions are transforming energy access across Latin America and the Caribbean.

LAC is uniquely positioned for a low-carbon transition. Renewable energy investments have soared, with solar and wind driving new capacity installations. However, fossil fuels still account for 66% of primary energy supply in the entire region and over 90% in the Caribbean.

Scaling renewables is not only about decarbonization 💬️ for he region – it's an engine for job creation and industrial transformation. The region could generate millions of green jobs if policy, finance, and local innovation are aligned. ECLAC estimates that 1.33% of GDP annually from 2021-2032 could make energy sources 86% renewable and cut GHG emissions by 30%.

Additionally,

content.title: In Energy Efficiency: Despite a 17% drop in energy intensity over 30 years, efficiency gains are slow. The building and transport sectors are ripe for scalable improvements.
In Green Hydrogen Potential: With low-cost renewables, LAC can become a global green hydrogen hub. Countries like Chile, Brazil, and Uruguay are leading with over 25 pilot projects under development.

metadata.title: Scenarios for green jobs creation in Latin America and the Caribbean, 2020-2030
metadata.footnote: Notes: LAC countries included are Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Mexico, Paraguay and Uruguay. The data refer to an unweighted average over the countries’ forecasts. Green sectors are defined in each country by first identifying the number of green tasks that workers perform in their occupations and then by examining the top ten industries across which those jobs are distributed. The baseline scenario assumes that, in each green sector, value added and employment will follow the same dynamic as in the past ten years. The counterfactual scenarios are defined according to the impact of a green policy that aims to boost investment in fixed and human capital, with a positive impact on value‑added growth in each green sector. The high‑impact scenario assumes that the value added in each sector will increase by 3 percentage points per year, adjusting to the new equilibrium. The medium‑impact scenario assumes that the value added will increase by 2 percentage points per year, while the low‑impact scenario assumes it will decrease by 1 percentage point per year. In all forecasts, total factor productivity will increase by 1 percentage point due to lower climate damages and new technology‑induced change. Employment change is forecast using the estimated short‑term elasticity to the value added, applying a panel dynamic model, defined by each sector and country, in the last ten years. Sources: Authors’ estimates based on Labour Force Surveys, National Accounts data by industries, (Vona et al., 2018[13]) and (Hardy, Keister and Lewandowski, 2018[14]).

content.text: The region lags others in terms of renewable energy production. However, there is promise to be found in the region’s increasing capacity for renewables, which has multiplied tenfold over the past decade.

content.title: The total installed renewable energy capacity is at 23.6 GW, with 5.1 GW added from just 2018 to 2020.
content.body: The capacity increase has been concentrated in a few countries, such as Egypt, Jordan, and Morocco. It also has been mostly for PV, with capacity more than doubling from 3.2 GW in 2018 to 7.4 GW by the end of 2020. Wind energy and CSP saw only minor increases. Perhaps unexpectedly, oil-producing countries have also increasingly turned to solar to supply local electricity, with several mega-scale projects under development. This is part of efforts to conserve oil and gas reserves for future export revenues.

content.text: Four key priority areas have been identified for the region

a. Closing the Energy Access Gap
Enhancing energy access is directly linked to reducing multidimensional poverty. Households with energy access experience improved educational outcomes, health, and productivity.
Digital payment models (e.g., pay-as-you-go solar) and community-led electrification are scalable across off-grid and rural areas.

b. Accelerating a Just Energy Transition
Transitioning to renewables could cut emissions by 30% and make the energy mix 86% renewable by 2032 with just 1.33% of GDP annual investment.
It also creates gender-responsive employment opportunities and reduces inequality if designed inclusively.

c. Strengthening Energy Resilience
Caribbean states spend up to 1.2% of GDP on natural disaster recovery annually. resilient infrastructure 💬️ – especially solar mini-grids – can protect critical services during disasters.

d. Driving Energy Finance and Investment
Only 1.3% of regional GDP goes to fossil fuel subsidies, a significant fiscal burden. Redirecting subsidies to clean investments could generate better returns, equity, and environmental benefits.
Regional development banks and local financial institutions (with nearly $1 trillion in assets) are crucial for unlocking blended finance and de-risking projects.
Globally, clean energy investments reached $1.3 trillion in 2022, but only a small share goes to Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC), which needs $125–200 billion annually to meet SDG 7 targets.

Innovative tools like blended finance, <ai prompt="Provide more info on green bonds.">green bonds 💬️</ai>, and concessional loans—backed by public funding through mechanisms such as the GEF and GCF—are vital to mobilize private capital. National development banks also play a crucial role. Well-structured finance can catalyze inclusive development by supporting energy access, productivity, e-mobility, climate-resilient agriculture, and circular economies.

takeaways.title: Energy Poverty Persists in Marginalized Areas, especially in the Caribbean and Rural Zones. While LAC reports a high overall electricity access rate (97.6%), over 17 million people remain without electricity, and 78 million still lack access to clean cooking, with the Caribbean and Indigenous communities facing the deepest gaps.

The Region Has One of the World’s Cleanest Grids but Still Relies Heavily on Fossil Fuels LAC generates more than 60% of its electricity from renewables, particularly hydropower, yet fossil fuels still dominate the overall energy mix (66%), especially in transport and industry
Unlocking Finance and Building Resilience Are Central to a Just Energy Transition The region requires $125–200 billion annually to meet SDG 7 targets and build climate-resilient energy systems.
